To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

droughts and epidemic diseases were recurrent phenomena in the pre-colonial history of Sudanic West Africa; that they were not necessarily ‘natural disasters’ in that they were often caused by a combination of climatic and human-induced factors; that they turned into disasters in the form of famine when the social and political structures were not able to cope with the stress caused by the climatic and/or epidemic crisis.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the causes of disasters are not natural, but that the impact of droughts and epidemic diseases on human populations can be considered as natural disasters.

the history of pre-colonial droughts and epidemias is still in its infancy and that the history of disaster is not only the history of a natural hazard, but a complex process of interaction between nature and society.

The main takeaway from our work is that
droughts, famines and epidemics have to be understood as historical events, and not just as natural disasters.
the history of pre-colonial droughts and epidemices in Sudanic Africa is a history of the interplay of climate, society and politics.
the history of disasters is an important field of research for Africanists, but it is not a field that can be studied without the necessary historical contextualisation of the events.
